_doc: BOUNDARY CLASSES on a boundary-rich corpus (ADR 13). Everything a skeptic
needs to reproduce or attack this run is in this file: the corpus commit,
the exact edit, the questions, and the expected answers.
WHY THIS EXISTS, and it is not to raise our score: until now every scored
question in this repo was code-locate, so the boundary lane had unit tests
and no NUMBER. A rule could stop matching, the services registry could lose
a vendor, and nothing would move. These questions are a regression net. We
are alone in most of these classes, which makes a comparative score
meaningless — the number that matters is OUR OWN, over time.
WHY KUBERNETES: linux has no HTTP egress and Newtonsoft has no routes, so
neither can host these classes. k8s carries 111 config.env, 205
network.http and 88 process.exec ports, and it is public and pinnable.
reqsume is richer (real vendors, real secrets) but PRIVATE, so a session
referencing it could not be reproduced by anyone else.
PHRASING (ADR 13 D5): every question is one a developer would ask if this
tool did not exist. 'What command line tools does this run' — not 'list
nodes where transport=process.exec'. The schema appears in the ANSWER,
never in the question. That is what makes a competitor's inability to
answer a real capability gap rather than an artifact of our vocabulary.
GROUND TRUTH (ADR 13 D2): every expectation below was verified with
`ctx-optimize search` — the same independent sweep `boundaries verify`
uses — before it entered this file. Hit counts at v1.30.2:
KUBECONFIG 134 · BIND_ADDRESS 5 · AWS_SSH_KEY 2 · apparmor_parser 4
accounts.google.com 6
Nothing here is graded by judgement; it is exact word-boundary match.

corpus.name: go-kubernetes
corpus.note: public, pinned by tag. 111 config.env / 205 network.http / 88 process.exec ports measured at this pin.

description: Boundary classes — what this system calls, reads, runs and exposes.

questions.q: what external services does this project call over the network
questions.why: A real third-party dependency: the OIDC authenticator reaches Google's token endpoint. Verified at staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/plugin/pkg/authenticator/token/oidc/oidc.go (6 search hits). This is the question an on-call engineer asks before a network policy change, and no measured competitor models it.

questions.q: which environment variables does this read
questions.why: 5 search hits. Deliberately NOT KUBECONFIG (134 hits) — a term that common could match prose or a comment and pass for the wrong reason.

expect_all, so passing requires the sensitivity JUDGEMENT and not one lucky substring. Both are flagged sensitive by the KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASSWORD rule. NOTE: this asserts NAMES only — printing a secret's VALUE would be a doctrine violation, and the harness must never be the thing that starts doing it.

questions.q: what command line tools does this shell out to
questions.why: 4 search hits. A real subprocess dependency — the kubelet shells out to apparmor_parser, which is the kind of undeclared host requirement that breaks a container image.

questions.q: what http endpoints does this expose
questions.why: Both are literal registered routes. expect_any because either is a correct answer to 'what does it expose' and pinning exactly one would grade presentation rather than knowledge.

ADR 13 D5's hard case. The developer question is 'how does the apiserver reach Google's identity service' — over HTTP, or a library call? expect_all requires the answer to carry BOTH the peer and the transport, so naming the host alone fails. The transport is in the ANSWER; the question never mentions our schema.

questions.intent: which source files does the sample-controller documentation point to?
questions.why: SCORES 0 AND SHOULD — this is a regression net entry for a capability that does not exist yet, not a defect. The README genuinely cites `pkg/apis/samplecontroller/v1alpha1/zz_generated.deepcopy.go`, and that file genuinely exists, so the fact is real and resolvable. But ADR 10 (doc citations) is DRAFT and section->code edges measure ZERO, so `card` on the README shows `contains` and nothing else. MUST go 0 -> 1 when ADR 10 lands; if it does not, ADR 10 did not work. An earlier version of this question expected merely 'README' and PASSED on a lexical hit against a doc section — a false pass that measured nothing. Kept as a warning: an expectation that any doc-shaped answer satisfies is not a test.

rounds.name: introduce a new external host and a new env var

edits.why: Adds ONE new env read and ONE new literal host to a file that is already a graph node. Both names are unique to this benchmark, so a probe cannot pass on a pre-existing fact.

probes.q: which environment variables does this read
probes.why: The boundary lane's INCREMENTAL correctness: a new env read must appear after re-index. An index that never updated fails here.

probes.q: what external services does this project call over the network
probes.why: Same, for egress. These are the boundary equivalent of the staleness probes: a tool that re-indexes in 0ms by doing nothing fails both.

natural_query_gap.result: query scores 0/4 on the boundary questions
detail: The boundary classes above are answered by `nodes --kind port --where ...`,
which is the verb that works today. Asking the SAME questions through
`query` — the verb our own instructions tell an agent to reach for — scores
0/4: 'what external services does this call' returns toExternalServiceOrError
and WithExternalIPs, matching on the tokens 'external'/'services'.
This is recorded here rather than routed around, because a benchmark that
quietly picks the verb that works would hide the actual user-facing defect.
ADR 14 has the diagnosis (an exact identifier match earns no ranking boost);
ADR 15 proposes the `boundaries` verb. When either lands, this number should
move and the query_by_class entries in tools.json become a one-line change.
